newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Rich north plundering poor south, 'P7' says.
newsitem.headline: Rich north plundering poor south, 'P7' says.

text.p: Leading figures from seven of the world's poorest countries and European Green parliamentarians on Wednesday accused the rich north of pushing developing nations further into poverty and plundering their natural resources.

"Poverty does not come out of giving little. Poverty comes out of taking away the means of livelihood and survival of people," Vananda Shiva of India's Research Foundation for Science, Technology and Natural Resource Policy told a news conference held to launch a meeting between Euro-MPs and representatives from the seven poor nations.

As the meeting began, the European Parliament legal affairs committee approved a European Commission proposal to allow multinational food and drug companies to patent the active properties of plants from developing nations.

"This is giving licence to take the last resource that allows people to survive in the third world, which is their biodiversity and their knowledge of how to use it for nutrition, for health care and all the other needs," he said.

The so-called P7 summit, organised by Greens in the EU assembly, was timed to coincide with the June 20-21 summit in the United States of the G7, the world's seven leading economic powers, and Russia.
Shiva criticised G7 plans for a multinational accord on the protection of foreign investment.
He said it would give foreign corporations the right to sue the governments of developing countries if they tried to regulate investment for health, education or environmental reasons.

German Green Euro-MP Wilfried Telkamper said the world's rich nations had pushed relentlessly for free trade and profits at the expense of developing nations, where poverty and unemployment had more than doubled in the last 20 years.
He said the G7 should start tackling more seriously a problem for which it was largely responsible.
The P7 summit is due on Friday to agree on a declaration highlighting the roots of impoverishment in the developing world and proposals for tackling it.
It would be forwarded to EU governments and provide the basis of a joint north-south strategy for fighting inequality, Belgian Green Euro-MP Paul Lannoye told Reuters.

In the runup to the G7 summit, which will devote some attention to the developing world, the European Commission issued a document on Wednesday saying that the EU offered more aid and trade assistance to poor nations than the United States or Japan.
While acknowledging EU efforts, Telkamper said the Union planned to cut spending on aid in 1998 and had consistently failed to address the problem of Third World debt.
